paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: belonging to the LORD is not a casual thing. A man or a woman could make the vow of a Nazirite, and that means the door was open to anybody, not just the priests (Numbers 6:2). The vow was about being separated to the LORD, and the text says that throughout his separation, "he is holy to the LORD" (Numbers 6:8). Being set apart was never about being impressive. It was about whose you are.

And the vow showed. The Nazirite carried what the text calls the symbol of consecration on his head, and that sign was worth guarding, even when it meant staying away from a family member who had died (Numbers 6:7). Now, if a sudden death defiled him, the road wasn't closed. Offerings were made to atone for him, and he could rededicate his time to the LORD, even though the earlier days no longer counted (Numbers 6:11-12). I'd be LOUD about restarting at day one, but I'd still take a way back over no way back.

Then comes the finish line, and the passage ends where it matters most: "he must fulfill whatever vow he makes" (Numbers 6:21). So here's what I want you to take to your own kitchen, baker. When you tell the LORD yes, mean it and stay with it until it's done. He is the One who gave a way back, so you can keep going with a glad heart.
